lines.en: Hi Raj! How’s your first week?
lines.pt: Oi, Raj! Como está a sua primeira semana?

lines.en: Good! **I just started.** **I work in** sales.
lines.pt: Boa! Acabei de começar. Trabalho em vendas.
A que horas começa a reunião da equipe?

lines.en: At ten a.m., in room two.

lines.en: Thanks. **Can I borrow** a laptop for the meeting?

pages.title: Real-Life Mission Day 6

situation.text: It is your first week at a new job in the United States. In one day you meet people, check the schedule, borrow something, write an email and make a short call.

pages.goal: By the end of the class you can survive a first week at work: introduce yourself, ask about times, borrow things, write a short email and close politely.
canDo: Introduce yourself: I just started. I work in…
Ask about time: What time does… start?
Borrow and request: Can I borrow…? / Could you send…?
Write and thank: I’m writing to… Thanks for your help.
success: I ask about a time or a place.
I borrow or request something politely.
I write or say a polite closing.

pages.title: Cultural snapshot — Life in the USA
pages.intro: A first week at work in the United States uses everything in this unit. Look at the cards and guess before you read.

cards.note: First names are common; “Ms.” and “Mr.” are for formal moments.
People say 10 a.m., not 10:00; always check a.m. or p.m.
Hi + name, a clear request and “Best,” are enough at most workplaces.

qs.q: What helps in a first week at work?
qs.pt: O que ajuda na primeira semana de trabalho?

levels.A2: Say hello, ask simple questions and say thank you.
levels.B1: Introduce yourself, ask questions without fear and thank people for their help.
levels.B2: Being friendly, asking for clarification early and thanking people build good relationships quickly.

qs.q: Is it okay to ask for repetition at work?
qs.pt: Pode pedir para repetir no trabalho?

levels.B1: Yes, it is normal and polite to ask for repetition.
levels.B2: It shows you want to get it right, so people usually appreciate it.

qs.q: How do you thank a colleague?

levels.B1: “Thanks for your help” in speech, “Thanks, Best” in email.
levels.B2: A short, sincere thanks fits better than a long speech.

pages.compare: In Brazil you may go out for lunch with new colleagues quickly. In the US it can be quicker or slower, depending on the company. How was it for you?

pages.title: Pronunciation lab — natural American English
pages.tip: In fast speech, “Could you” sounds like “couldja” and “Can I” like “ca-nI”. Understand them and use them when you feel ready.

pages.title: Writing — a small real-life task
pages.task: Write a short email to your manager at the end of your first week. Thank the team and ask for next week’s schedule.

pages.title: Level up — the same situation from A1 to C2
pages.intro: You do not need six different methods: the structure stays, while language complexity and autonomy grow.

ladder.say: Hello. I work. Meeting, what time?
ladder.goal: Get through the day with words and gestures.

ladder.say: I just started. What time does the meeting start? Can I borrow a laptop?
I just started last week, so could you send me the schedule when you have a minute?
Since I’m still getting to know the team, I’d really appreciate it if you could walk me through next week.
I’d be grateful for any pointers as I settle in; so far the team has been very welcoming.
I’m conscious that I’m still finding my feet, so I would welcome any guidance you might offer.
ladder.goal: Use a refined, tactful professional register.

pages.note: This progression is illustrative: complex sentences do not define a level on their own. CEFR also considers comprehension, autonomy, fluency, accuracy, interaction and appropriateness.
